Jagannath of Puri

Temple Stories

Jagannath of Puri

From the search for Nilamadhava to the consecration

In everyday English — Skanda Purana, Purushottama-mahatmya

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This is the story of a search. A king sets out to find God — first in the forest, then on the shore of the sea, then behind the closed door of his own temple. Where there is searching, read slowly; where God is found, let joy into your voice.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — the king grave, Vidyapati humble, Narada sweet, Brahma calm.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The main story of this book is from the Purushottama-mahatmya of the Skanda Purana — King Indradyumna, the search for Nilamadhava, the divine log, and the unfinished forms. The Brahma Purana tells the same story with small differences. Where something comes from a later or local telling, it is given separately in a note — never blended into the main story. All the sources are named separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Indradyumna — king of Malava (Avanti). A great devotee of Vishnu. His heart is not filled by gold or silver, but by the sight of God.

Vidyapati — a Brahmin, the younger brother of the king's royal priest. He goes into the forest to find Nilamadhava.

Vishvavasu — chief of the Sabara people. He worships Nilamadhava in a hidden cave in the forest.

Lalita — Vishvavasu's daughter, Vidyapati's wife. Clever and kind.

Nilamadhava — the blue Vishnu worshipped on the blue mountain — the same god who later is called Jagannath at Puri.

Gundicha — Queen of Indradyumna. She is the one who asked for the carpenter's door to be opened.

Narada — the divine sage. Elderly, long white beard, hair in a topknot, bare chest, saffron robes, veena in hand.

Brahma — the creator. Four heads, long white beard, seated on a pink lotus.

Vishwakarma — the divine craftsman of the gods. He comes in the disguise of an old carpenter to carve the forms.

Jagannath — the dark, almost black wooden form, large round eyes, broad smile, no hands, no feet. He sits in the middle.

Balabhadra — Jagannath's elder brother. Fair and white, the same shape.

Subhadra — the younger sister of the two brothers. Yellow, smaller, between her brothers.

Sudarshana — the discus, a fourth form carved from the same wood.

1 · The King's Dream · · THE KING'S DREAM

This is a very old story — from the Satya Yuga. In the land of Malava ruled King Indradyumna. The king had everything — gold, elephants, an army, a great palace. But his heart was set on one thing only — the sight of God.

One day a traveller came to the king's court. He had wandered far and wide. He told a wondrous thing — “In the land of Odra, on the blue mountain, there is a god — Nilamadhava. The blue Vishnu. The Sabara chief Vishvavasu worships him in a cave in the forest, hidden from all. Whoever sees him finds peace of heart.”

The king heard this — and could not rest. That night he dreamed — the blue god standing on the blue mountain, looking at him and smiling. In the morning the king decided — “I shall see Nilamadhava.”

The king sent his Brahmins in all four directions — “Go, find Nilamadhava.” All of them returned — none had found anything. Only one did not return — Vidyapati, the younger brother of the royal priest.

The king said — “Vidyapati is my last hope. If he returns, it means God has called.”

(Read this slowly — let the king's longing be heard.)

Pause and think — The king had everything — yet he set out to find God. Do things ever fill the heart? And one traveller's tale lit a fire in the king's heart — has a single thing someone said ever lit such a longing in your heart too?

2 · Vidyapati's Search · · VIDYAPATI'S SEARCH

Vidyapati walked on and on until he reached the forest of Odra. There he found a village of the Sabaras. The chief of the village was Vishvavasu — tall, plain-spoken, a devotee of God. He gave Vidyapati shelter in his house.

In the house lived Vishvavasu's daughter, Lalita. Vidyapati and Lalita took a liking to each other. Vishvavasu married them. Vidyapati now lived in that house — but his heart stayed on the search.

Vidyapati noticed one thing — every evening Vishvavasu left the house, and returned only the next day at noon. When he returned, his clothes carried the fragrance of flowers and sandalwood.

Vidyapati asked Lalita — “Where does your father go every evening?”

Lalita said softly — “He goes to worship Nilamadhava — in a cave in the forest. The place is secret — only our people know it.”

Vidyapati begged Lalita — “Let me see him once.” Lalita spoke to her father — and Vishvavasu agreed, on one condition — “You must walk blindfolded. The way must be told to no one.”

Lalita was clever. She tied a small pouch of mustard seeds to Vidyapati's clothes — with a tiny hole in it. As he walked, the seeds fell along the path.

When they reached the cave the blindfold was opened — before them stood Nilamadhava — deep blue, calm, smiling. Vidyapati folded his hands and bowed.

Pause and think — Lalita helped her husband — but she did not break her father's trust either; she kept the way hidden and only dropped the seeds. Are there many ways to help? And walking blindfolded — is that a sign of trust, or of fear?

3 · Nilamadhava Vanishes · · NILAMADHAVA VANISHES

Vidyapati returned to Malava and told the king everything — the cave, Nilamadhava, the mustard seeds. The king danced with joy. He set out for Odra with a great retinue and his family.

The rains had passed. Wherever the seeds had fallen, mustard plants had grown — green and lush, showing the way. The king followed that path to the cave —

but the cave was empty. Nilamadhava had vanished. It is said the god had hidden himself beneath the sand. The king's heart broke.

The king said — “I came so far — and God met me, yet did not meet me?”

The king did not give up. He stayed on the blue mountain — fasting, praying. Then a divine voice was heard —

The divine voice said — “King, do not grieve. I have hidden myself as Nilamadhava — but I shall come to you as wood, from the sea. Wait on the shore of the sea.”

The king began to build a temple on the blue mountain — and kept looking toward the sea.

Pause and think — The king found the way, yet did not find God — God had hidden himself. Does God ever hide — or do we lose the eyes to see him? And the king did not give up, but prayed — is not giving up also a kind of worship?

4 · The Divine Log · · THE DIVINE LOG

One morning there was a stir on the shore of the sea. A great log of wood was floating in on the waves — fragrant neem wood, marked with the signs of the conch and the discus. It was no ordinary wood — it was Daru Brahma — Brahman in the form of wood.

The king ran to the shore. The people brought the log ashore with great reverence. The king said — “This is the form the voice spoke of.”

Now the question was — who would carve forms from this sacred wood? The king called master sculptors from many lands. But the moment anyone set a chisel to the wood, the edge of the chisel went blunt. The wood would not cut at all.

The sculptors said — “Your Majesty, this wood is beyond us. Only a divine hand can carve it.”

The king grew worried — the wood had come, but no one could carve it.

Pause and think — The wood floated in — no one cut it, no one sent it. Does God choose the way of his own coming? And the sculptors' chisels went blunt — is every work not for every hand — must some works wait for the right hand?

5 · The Old Carpenter · · THE OLD CARPENTER

Then an old carpenter came to the court — white beard, bent back, chisel and hammer in hand. He said — “Your Majesty, I can carve these forms.”

The king asked — “Who are you, old father?” The old man smiled and said — “Only a carpenter, Your Majesty. But I have one condition — I shall work for twenty-one days in a closed room. No one shall open the door, no one shall peep inside.”

The king said — “As you wish, old father. For twenty-one days no one shall open the door.”

The door closed. From inside came the sound of chisel and hammer — tap-tap, tap-tap. Every day the king stood outside the door and listened.

The first week passed, the second week passed — the sound kept coming. Then one day the sound stopped. One day passed, two days passed — no sound from inside.

Queen Gundicha grew afraid — “The old father has been in a closed room for so many days — no food, no water. What if he has died?” She said to the king — “Open the door and look.”

Pause and think — The old carpenter set a condition — and the king accepted it. Is keeping a promise also devotion? And the queen asked for the door to be opened — out of kindness. Can kindness also become a mistake — when it breaks a promise?

6 · The Unfinished Forms · · THE UNFINISHED FORMS

The king opened the door — and no one was inside. The old carpenter had vanished.

Before them stood three forms — unfinished. Large round eyes, a broad smile — but no hands had been made, no feet. The wooden forms were only half carved.

The king's heart filled. He wept — “I broke my promise. The carpenter has gone — and God is left unfinished.”

Then the sage Narada came — veena in hand, a calm smile on his face. He placed his hand on the king's shoulder.

Narada said — “King, do not weep. The old carpenter who came was no ordinary carpenter — he was Vishwakarma himself, the craftsman of the gods.”

“And these forms are not unfinished — God has chosen this very form. Without hands he still embraces everyone, without feet he still reaches everyone.”

That very night the king heard a divine voice — “I wish to remain in this form. Install them just as they are.”

About the Counting of the Days

Some tellings say the carpenter's condition was twenty-one days and the door was opened around the fifteenth day; some say the condition itself was fifteen days. This book follows the main telling of a twenty-one-day condition — the other count is given here separately, not blended into the main story.

Pause and think — God looked unfinished — but Narada said, he is not unfinished. Is only what is complete beautiful — or can the unfinished also be complete, if it is God's will? And the king broke his promise — yet God forgave him. Is forgiveness also a form of God?

7 · The Consecration · · THE CONSECRATION

Now the king had one wish — that Brahma himself, the creator, should consecrate these forms. The king went to Brahmaloka and invited Brahma to come to Puri.

Brahma came — four heads, long white beard, seated on a pink lotus. He saw the temple — and was pleased.

With mantras, flowers and water, Brahma performed the consecration of the three forms. It is said that in that very moment life entered the wood.

The three forms were enthroned on the jewelled throne — Jagannath in the middle — dark, almost black, large round eyes, broad smile; Balabhadra on one side — fair and white, the same shape; little Subhadra between them — yellow, between her two brothers. With them a fourth form — the Sudarshana discus — carved from the same wood.

Brahma said — “King, these forms are no longer only wood — God dwells in them. Whoever sees them will find peace of heart.”

The king folded his hands and said — “Lord, my temple is now complete.”

The Story of the Brahma-padartha

A popular later telling says that inside the form there is the Brahma-padartha — the heart of Shri Krishna, which did not burn on the pyre and came floating across the sea to Puri. This telling is not the main story of the Puranas — it is later tradition and local belief. So it is told here in a separate note, not blended into the main story.

Pause and think — Brahma himself came — the greatest of gods, to a king's temple. Does devotion draw even the greatest? And life entered the wood — when does a thing become sacred — when it is made — or when devotion dwells in it?

The story continues — the Rath Yatra, the Nabakalebara and the Mahaprasad — in 'Jagannath's Living Traditions'

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The main story of this book is from the Purushottama-mahatmya of the Skanda Purana (Vaishnava Khanda) — the story of Indradyumna, the search for Nilamadhava, the divine log, and the installation of the forms come from there.

Brahma Purana

The Brahma Purana (Part 2, chapters 41–47) tells the story of Indradyumna with small differences — it is this book's parallel source. Where the two differ, the Skanda Purana's telling has been followed as the main one.

Niladri Mahodaya

Niladri Mahodaya is a text describing the temple rites of Puri — it was used for the description of the consecration rites in this book.

The Search for Nilamadhava

Vidyapati staying in Vishvavasu's house, marrying Lalita, going to the cave blindfolded, dropping mustard seeds, and the way being found when the seeds sprouted — all of this is the story of the Purushottama-mahatmya. The god hiding himself by the time the king arrived is there too.

The Divine Log and the Old Carpenter

The fragrant log floating in from the sea, Vishwakarma coming as an old carpenter, the twenty-one-day condition, Queen Gundicha having the door opened, and the unfinished forms being found — this is the story of both the Skanda Purana and the Brahma Purana.

Consecration by Brahma

Brahma coming from Brahmaloka to consecrate the temple and the forms is in the story of the Skanda Purana.

Later Tellings — Kept Separate

The story of the Brahma-padartha (the heart of Shri Krishna) and the difference in the counting of the days — neither of these has been blended into the main story; each is told in its own note inside the book.

About the Pictures

In this book the three forms are shown as they are worshipped at Puri — large round eyes, broad smile, no hands, no feet. They are never shown 'completed' — the unfinished form is the heart of this story.
